The [[governor of Mississippi]] is the [[head of government]] of [[Mississippi]]. The [[Constitution of Mississippi]], ratified in 1890, calls for a four-year term for the governor,{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=2103|loc=1890 art. 5, § 116}} elected via the [[two-round system]] since a [[2020 Mississippi elections#Elimination of state electoral college|2020 referendum]].{{sfn|Miss. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/ms/constitution/section-id-72905 art. V, § 140]}} Prior to this, the governor was elected by an [[electoral college]] composed of the districts represented in the [[Mississippi House of Representatives]], with a [[contingent election]] held in the House in the event no candidate received a majority of district electors.{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=2075|loc=1868 art. V, § 2}} The term length was originally two years,{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=2039|loc=1817 art. IV, § 1}} with no limit on how many terms they could serve. The 1832 constitution limited governors to serving no more than four out of every six years.{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=2058|loc=1832 art. V, § 3}} When terms were lengthened to four years in 1868,{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=2075|loc=1868 art. V, § 1}} this limit was removed. The 1890 constitution forbid governors from succeeding themselves,{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=2103|loc=1890 art. 5, § 116}} but a 1986 amendment allows them to succeed themselves once.{{sfn|Miss. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/ms/constitution/section-id-72858 art. V, § 116]}} The office of the lieutenant governor was created in the 1817 constitution,{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=2040|loc=1817 art. IV, § 18}} abolished in 1832,{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=2059|loc=1868 art. V, § 17}} and recreated in 1868.{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=2076|loc=1868 art. V, § 14}} When the office of governor becomes vacant for any reason, the lieutenant governor exercises the powers of governor for the remainder of the term.{{sfn|Miss. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/ms/constitution/section-id-72889 art. V, § 131]}} The governor and the lieutenant governor are not officially elected on the same ticket.

The current governor is [[Mississippi Republican Party|Republican]] [[Tate Reeves]], who took office January 14, 2020.

== List of governors ==
=== Mississippi Territory ===
[[Mississippi Territory]] was organized on April 7, 1798, from land ceded to the federal government by [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]].<ref>{{usstat|1|549}}</ref> It had four governors appointed by the [[president of the United States]] during its 19-year history, including one, [[David Holmes (politician)|David Holmes]], who would later serve as state governor.

=== State of Mississippi ===
Mississippi was [[Admission to the Union|admitted to the Union]] on December 10, 1817.<ref>{{usstat|3|348}}, {{usstat|3|472}}</ref> It seceded from the [[Union (American Civil War)|Union]] on January 9, 1861,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Secession Ordinances of 13 Confederate States |url=http://www.digitalhistory.uh.edu/disp_textbook.cfm?smtID=3&psid=3953 |url-status=live |year=2018 |last1=Mintz |first1=S. |last2=McNeil |first2=S. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150905091739/http://www.digitalhistory.uh.edu/disp_textbook.cfm?smtID=3&psid=3953 |archive-date=September 5, 2015 |access-date=October 1, 2026 |website=Digital History}}</ref> and was a founding member of the [[Confederate States of America]] on February 4, 1861.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=dul1.ark:/13960/t2t44fh2r&seq=23 |page=1 |title=The Statutes at Large of the Provisional Government of the Confederate States of America |editor-last=Matthews |editor-first=James M. |year=1864 |location=Richmond, Virginia |publisher=R.M. Smith |via=[[HathiTrust]]}}</ref> During the [[Reconstruction era]] following the end of the [[American Civil War]], Mississippi was part of the [[Fourth Military District]], which exerted some control over governor appointments and elections. Mississippi was readmitted to the Union on February 23, 1870.<ref>{{usstat|16|67}}</ref>

|data-sort-value="731"|November 21, 1833{{efn|All sources, modern and older, say Runnels took office on November 20; however, contemporary news shows he was inaugurated on November 21.<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 6, 1833 |title=Mississippi Legislature |page=2 |newspaper=Natchez Courier |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-weekly-natchez-courier-runnels-inaug/121261067/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928043611/https://www.newspapers.com/article/121261067/runnels-inaugurated-nov-21/ |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |url-status=live |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref><ref name="interregnum">{{Cite news |date=November 27, 1835 |title=Interregnum |page=2 |newspaper=The Mississippian |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-weekly-mississippian-interregnum/121262465/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928045115/https://www.newspapers.com/article/121262465/interregnum/ |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |url-status=live |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>}}<br />–<br />November 21, 1835<br>{{small|(731 days; lost election)}}{{efn|The 1832 constitution specified that governor "shall hold his office for two years from the time of his installation;" thus, on November 21, 1835, two years after he took office, Runnels, having lost the 1835 election, left office. However, the legislature had set the start of the next term in January. The Senate met on December 3 and elected a new president, Quitman, who would act as governor until the governor-elect, Lynch, took office.{{sfn|Sobel|1978|p=806}}}}
